implementation_notes: The whole structure collapses into a Map from key to the in-flight Promise: look up the key, return the existing promise if present, otherwise start the call, store the promise synchronously (before any await, so no interleaving can start a second one) and delete it when it settles with .finally. Everything the classic implementation does with an entry, a wait queue and a broadcast is done by the promise itself: many callers may await the same promise, and its fulfilment or rejection is delivered to all of them. What still has to be written by hand is the key (tenant/scope included) and the deletion - the language gives no forget-on-completion for free.
pitfalls: Store the promise in the same synchronous turn in which it is created: an await between the lookup and the set lets a second caller miss the entry and start a duplicate.
Delete on settle, not only on fulfilment: a rejected promise left in the map is joined forever and the key can never be retried.
All waiters share the rejection - attach handling on every path; the recorded stack belongs to the leader, and an unhandled shared rejection also raises an unhandled-rejection warning.
A shared promise keeps its result and closure alive until it settles and the entry is deleted; unbounded key cardinality grows the registry, so bound it or bypass it under pressure.
Per-caller timeouts must not cancel the shared work: race the wait against a timer instead of passing one caller's AbortSignal into the shared fetch.

variants.name: DataLoader (batching loader with per-key promise cache)
variants.idiom_name: new DataLoader(batchLoadFn) with per-tick load() coalescing
variants.implementation_notes: DataLoader is the pattern packaged for JavaScript: load(key) returns a promise, calls occurring in the same tick are coalesced into one batchLoadFn call, and the loader also caches the resulting promise per key. It descends from Facebook's 2010 Loader API, and its README states the key-scope rule as library usage: a loader instance represents a unique cache and is typically created per request when different users can see different things. Choose it when you also want batching (N ids -> one query) and are ready to own the per-request lifetime.
pitfalls: A loader instance is a per-key promise cache: created at module scope it mixes users' data; create it per request (the README's own guidance).
batchLoadFn must return one element per key in the same order; a wrong shape silently assigns results to the wrong keys.
Batching is per tick: calls from later ticks are not coalesced with earlier ones unless the loader's cache still holds the key.
Keys are compared by Map identity or stringification: object keys must be canonicalised before load().
